title: The Simple View of Schooling Redux
author: Terry Underwood
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn (terryu.substack.com), September 23, 2026
summary: Terry Underwood argues that No Child Left Behind, and the Every Student Succeeds Act that carried forward its tiered definition of evidence, did lasting damage to early literacy instruction by admitting only experimental research into policy. He contends that this narrow epistemology forced reading to be theorized as a mechanical, sequential process, which in turn produced DIBELS-style monitoring of phonemes and fluency while comprehension went largely unassessed. The essay's central move is to link a research paradigm to a classroom paradigm: what could be counted became what was taught. Underwood notes that the federal Reading First Impact Study found no significant effect on comprehension, and that even the National Reading Panel's five pillars were cut down to three in practice. He then widens the critique to the politics of schooling, arguing that quick fixes appeal to those who never have to implement them and that teachers have been recast as technicians working with fidelity under supervision rather than as interpretive professionals. The piece closes by pointing to AI eye-tracking tools now being adopted by states as the latest extension of the phonics-first fiction, and promises a follow-up essay on why such tools cannot inform expert teacher judgment.
points: Underwood locates the root problem in ESSA's inherited tiers of evidence, which privilege experimental and quasi-experimental designs over sociocultural and interpretive research.
He argues that DIBELS-driven monitoring of phoneme segmentation, nonsense words and reading rate meant that what was tested became what was taught.
The federal Reading First Impact Study (Gamse et al., 2008) is cited as finding no statistically significant effect on reading comprehension.
Teaching is framed as interpretive, ethically bound work rather than algorithmic delivery, drawing on Giroux and Biesta.
State adoption of AI eye-tracking tools in 2026 is presented as a research-averse extension of the phonics-first assumption.
quotes: NCLB, however, planted a pup tent and admitted only experimentalists who valued control groups, treatment groups, and fidelity as ways to reduce complexity by stepping away from the concrete world. If you couldn’t count it and t-test it, it didn’t count.
We got DIBELS-driven progress monitoring which measured phoneme segmentation, nonsense-word fluency, and oral reading rate, with comprehension barely assessed, so what was tested was taught.

In reading research, counting must theorize reading as primarily a mechanical, sequential, technical, autonomous cognitive process. Text goes in, reading happens, comprehension comes back like a chemical reaction.

Teachers are unfortunately viewed as public workers doing technical work with fidelity under supervision (Giroux, 1985). Teaching, however, is interpretive work, not algorithmic, carried out by experienced experts with ethical obligations to children (Biesta, 2015).
Quick fixes for schooling appeal to those who don’t have to implement them, and implementation is always underfunded, disorganized, fast and furious, and usually contested.

In 2026, states from the east coast to the west coast are implementing AI eye-tracking tools in a misguided, research-aversive impulse to drive ever deeper into the fiction that phonics first improves comprehension later.
